newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Aznar says opposition undermining EMU bid.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Aznar says opposition undermining EMU bid.

text.p: Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar accused the main opposition Socialist party on Monday of trying to sabotage government efforts to qualify for the single European currency, due for launch in 1999.

Aznar said the Socialist party, headed by former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, was undermining a bid to impose fiscal austerity required to qualify for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) by urging protests against a public sector wage freeze.
"The Socialist party has invited its supporters to join these strikes and demonstrations," Aznar told a joint news conference with visiting Jordan's Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti.
"If you are asking me "Is that position working against our country's interest vis-a-vis European monetary union?', (I would say) definitely so," Aznar said.
Tens of thousands of people protested in Madrid on Saturday against a two-year pay freeze for public sector workers included in the conservative government's strict 1997 budget.
The budget is aimed at bringing the economy in line with the Maastricht Treaty convergence criteria for a single European currency in the hope Spain will be among the founders of EMU.
A Socialist party spokeswoman denied Aznar's accusations, saying the party had not called on supporters to attend the weekend demonstration and was not officially in favour or against the protests.
"The party did not call the demonstration and did not send an (official) representative," said the spokeswoman, who asked not to be identified.
Aznar also said Gonzalez had himself frozen public workers' wages for two years during the nearly 14 years he was in power.

Union leaders have called for a general strike in the near future and promised to block highways and stage other protests to force the government into talks on the wage freeze. They said new protest measures would be decided at a November 28 meeting.
But Aznar said on Monday he would not reconsider his wage policy. "This position is not going to be changed," he said.
